title: State of UK Business 2026: A Divided Economy
gist: A survey of over 2,300 UK business leaders finds headline confidence up to 87% while profit expectations fall (48% expecting growth, -8pp) and a third of firms plan to cut headcount, meaning optimism reflects survival rather than expected growth. The deeper split is a small cohort of growth-expecting, AI-forward firms pulling away from a much larger disengaged middle that identifies neither opportunities nor threats.

insights.claim: 87% of surveyed UK business leaders say they are confident about their business's prospects over the next 12 months, up 4 percentage points from 2025.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: Headline UK sentiment indices may overstate the recovery; don't take confidence prints at face value when positioning in UK domestic cyclicals.
insights.quote: 87% describe themselves as confident about their business's prospects over the next 12 months (+4pp from 2025 level)
insights.locator: At first glance, business leaders appear

insights.claim: Even as headline confidence rose, fewer UK leaders expect profits to grow (48%, down 8pp) and more expect profits to decline (28%, up 10pp) versus 2025.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: Profit expectations are deteriorating faster than sentiment surveys imply — a warning for UK earnings revisions.
insights.quote: fewer leaders expect their profits to grow (48%, -8pp from 2025) and more expect them to decline (28%, +10pp)
insights.locator: However, looking past the headline numbers

insights.claim: A third (33%) of UK businesses now plan to shrink headcount, up 10 percentage points year over year and narrowly overtaking the 31% planning to grow headcount.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: Net hiring intentions have flipped negative, a leading indicator for UK labour market softening and consumer spending.
insights.quote: A third (33%) of businesses now plan to shrink headcount (+10pp), narrowly overtaking the 31% planning to grow it, which is unchanged on last year.
insights.locator: When it comes to workforce size

insights.claim: Rising business optimism reflects relief that 2025 was a particularly poor year and leaders' belief in their ability to cope, rather than any expectation that conditions will improve.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: Base-effect optimism is fragile and can reverse on the first shock; treat improving UK survey deltas as low-quality signal.
insights.quote: That is a thinner, more precarious, form of optimism than the headline number implies
insights.locator: Taken together, this suggests something other

insights.claim: What UK leaders say at the top line diverges systematically from what they actually plan to do, a say-do gap that is the central finding of the 2026 survey.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: Weight capex, hiring and adoption behaviour over stated sentiment when reading UK corporate surveys.
insights.locator: That distinction between what leaders say at the top line

themes.theme: Recession conviction concentrated in large firms

insights.claim: 57% of UK business leaders expect a recession, unchanged from last year, and even 57% of leaders who describe themselves as confident about the year ahead still expect one.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: Confidence and recession expectations coexist, so UK confidence readings carry little information about growth expectations.
insights.quote: Recession fears have not improved from last year (57%, flat) and even the majority (57%) of leaders who are confident about the year ahead still expect a recession.
insights.locator: Recession fears have not improved

insights.claim: The biggest businesses (60%, +6pp) and multinationals (61%, +5pp) are now the groups most convinced a UK recession could happen, despite normally being the least bearish and having the best visibility into global markets.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: When the best-informed cohort turns most bearish, it is a higher-quality recession signal than aggregate sentiment — watch UK-exposed large caps' guidance.
insights.quote: these businesses have the greatest visibility into global markets and tend to be least bearish on this front
insights.locator: It is also now the biggest businesses

themes.theme: Three-speed economy and the stagnant middle

insights.claim: Grouping firms by their own growth expectations rather than treating them as one block reveals three distinct behavioural cohorts: growth-expecting, decline-expecting and a flat middle.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: A segmentation lens that separates corporate winners from laggards is more useful than aggregate macro averages for stock selection.
insights.locator: sits at the heart of this year's findings

insights.claim: The three most frequently cited business opportunities across the whole sample were investing in new technology, using everyday AI tools and deploying agentic AI.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: Enterprise tech and agentic AI budgets are the top self-identified growth lever for UK firms — supportive for software and AI tooling demand.
insights.quote: the three opportunities mentioned most often were investing in new technology, using everyday AI tools and deploying agentic AI
insights.locator: Across the whole sample, the three opportunities

insights.claim: Firms expecting to shrink look outward for relief — hoping for tax changes, lower costs or lighter regulation — rather than pursuing technology opportunities themselves.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: Declining firms are policy-dependent rather than self-help driven, making them poor candidates for an operational turnaround thesis.
insights.locator: which instead tend to look outward

insights.claim: Businesses expecting to stay roughly the same size are the least engaged group of all — the least likely to identify an opportunity, a threat or a barrier at all.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: The drag on UK productivity is disengagement, not distress — which means neither stimulus nor cost relief will move it.
insights.quote: they are the group least likely to identify an opportunity, a threat or a barrier at all
insights.locator: There is a third group, however

insights.claim: Separate BCG research shows the tail of low-productivity UK businesses has lengthened and widened over the past two decades even as top performers held firm.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: UK aggregate productivity weakness is a distribution problem, so frontier-firm earnings can stay strong while national growth stays weak.
insights.quote: the tail of low-productivity businesses in the UK has lengthened and widened over the past two decades, even as its top performers held firm
insights.locator: It is a phenomenon that aligns with our separate research

insights.claim: The stagnant middle, far larger in number than frontier firms, is where UK growth policy should be focused if stagnant productivity growth is to be addressed.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: Watch for UK policy pivoting from frontier-firm incentives to broad-based diffusion programmes — a different set of beneficiaries.
insights.locator: That stagnant middle, far larger in number

themes.theme: Policy asks and the government trust deficit

insights.claim: Tax has topped the UK business policy wish list in every year of the survey, with business taxes (33%, -9pp), energy costs (27%, -10pp) and employment taxes (25%, -3pp) the top three priorities in 2026.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: Tax and energy costs remain the binding constraints UK firms cite, so budget decisions on those lines are the highest-beta policy events for UK domestics.
insights.quote: Business taxes (33%, -9pp), energy costs (27%, -10pp) and employment taxes (25%, -3pp) are still the three most-cited priorities
insights.locator: When it comes to what leaders want from government

insights.claim: Half of UK leaders (50%, +6pp) now think the government is prioritising the economy, yet 64% still rate its overall impact as negative, 66% think its spending priorities are wrong, and 73% say policy uncertainty is denting business confidence.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: Perceived intent has improved but trust has not, so policy uncertainty remains a live discount on UK corporate investment.
insights.quote: 64% (-3pp) still rate the government's overall impact as negative, 66% think its spending priorities are wrong and 73% say policy uncertainty is denting business confidence
insights.locator: There is some improvement in how leaders see

insights.claim: 52% of leaders feel more confident than they did three months earlier, which may reflect a new government still being sized up rather than a settled judgement.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: The recent confidence uptick is provisional and reversible on the first disappointing policy decision.
insights.locator: Leaders' confidence has also moved a little

themes.theme: AI enthusiasm concentrated among incumbents of adoption

insights.claim: 72% of leaders are personally positive about AI (34% strongly positive) and 75% now see it benefiting their own business, up 16 percentage points from 2025 and rising every year since 2024.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: Enterprise AI sentiment is still compounding rather than plateauing, supporting continued adoption-driven spend.
insights.quote: The share that sees it benefiting their own business has risen every year we have asked since 2024 and now stands at 75% (+16pp from 2025).
insights.locator: Sentiment here looks unambiguously positive

insights.claim: AI positivity is concentrated among those already furthest along: C-level leaders are far more positive than founders (84% vs. 58%), and daily users vastly more positive than occasional users (95% vs. 19%).
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: The 19% vs 95% gap means aggregate AI sentiment numbers are driven by a usage-selected minority — adoption depth, not headline enthusiasm, is the metric to track.
insights.quote: daily users are far more positive than occasional ones (95% vs. 19%)
insights.locator: C-level leaders are considerably more positive than founders

insights.claim: Greater AI usage and engagement leads to more positivity about the technology, not less — contradicting the idea that hands-on experience breeds disillusionment.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: Argues against an enterprise AI disillusionment cycle; churn risk in AI tooling may be lower than sceptics assume.
insights.quote: Greater AI usage and engagement leads to more positivity about the technology, not less.
insights.locator: Greater AI usage and engagement leads

insights.claim: 54% of growth-expecting firms cite improved quality of products or services as a reason for using AI, versus 36% of flat-profit firms and 31% of decline-expecting firms, an 18-23pp gap; on every other reason tested the three groups converge closely.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: The differentiator is intent about business outcomes, not usage volume — screen AI-adopting companies on stated outcome, not deployment headcount.
insights.quote: Over half (54%) of growth-expecting firms cite improved quality of products or services, against just over a third (36%) of firms expecting flat profit and 31% of firms expecting profit to decline
insights.locator: Growth-expecting firms are considerably more likely

insights.claim: Asked what they would do with a hypothetical 30% time saving from AI, growth-expecting firms said they would expand into new markets or reinvest in more AI, while decline-expecting firms were twice as likely to cut headcount or freeze hiring.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: The same AI productivity gain produces expansion at one cohort and labour cuts at another, so AI's net employment effect depends on firm trajectory, not the technology.
insights.quote: Decline-expecting firms were twice as likely to say they would use the same gain to cut headcount or freeze hiring instead
insights.locator: We also tested how leaders would react to a hypothetical windfall

themes.theme: AI self-assessment blind spot and non-adopters

insights.claim: 53% of leaders believe their business is ahead of competitors on AI while only 10% admit to being behind, a split that cannot be true in aggregate and implies widespread misjudgement of actual standing.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: Corporate self-reported AI leadership is close to worthless as evidence; demand third-party or outcome-based verification of AI positioning claims.
insights.quote: More than half of leaders (53%) believe their business is ahead of competitors on AI, while only one in ten (10%) admit to being behind, a split that simply cannot be true as a whole.
insights.locator: Self-perception adds another layer

insights.claim: If AI policy support depends on businesses first recognising they need help, it risks flowing to firms already ahead while passing over those that would gain most.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: Demand-led AI subsidy schemes will likely widen the productivity gap rather than close it — a second-order reason UK aggregate productivity may keep disappointing.
insights.locator: This is a problem if policy support depends

insights.claim: Firms that see themselves as ahead on AI report practical obstacles — security, cost, regulation and skills — while those that see themselves as behind report not knowing what AI would do for them or where to begin.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: The laggard bottleneck is use-case discovery, not budget, so services and enablement, not cheaper tokens, unlock the long tail of demand.
insights.locator: The obstacles each group reports are consistent

insights.claim: Cost is cited by fewer than a third of businesses overall as an AI obstacle, suggesting that by the time cost matters most firms have already concluded AI is worth having.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: Price is not the gating factor for enterprise AI adoption, which weakens the bear case built on AI being too expensive to deploy broadly.
insights.quote: Cost, despite the attention it gets externally, is cited by fewer than a third of businesses overall
insights.locator: Cost, despite the attention it gets externally

insights.claim: Among businesses not using AI at all, 53% say the idea has simply not crossed their mind; the top reasons given are that AI is not relevant to their line of work (47%) and a preference for keeping things human (45%), with cost far behind at 12%.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: Half the non-adopter market is untouched by awareness, implying a long runway of latent demand that marketing and distribution — not product — will unlock.
insights.quote: More than half (53%) say the idea has simply not crossed their mind.
insights.locator: That gap looks even wider among businesses not using AI

insights.claim: BCG's own analysis puts the baseline gain from current basic AI tools at 14% across broadly transferable tasks across the economy, implying the 'not relevant to us' view held by non-adopters does not stand up.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: A 14% economy-wide baseline uplift from already-available tools quantifies the unclaimed productivity pool sitting with non-adopters.
insights.quote: our own analysis of the wider economic opportunity from AI put the baseline gain from current basic AI tools at 14% across broadly transferable tasks across the economy
insights.locator: On the relevance point specifically

insights.claim: The gap between firms capturing value from AI and the rest is already stark and likely to widen further without targeted intervention.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: Expect widening dispersion in corporate margins and productivity — favours a barbell of AI-capturing frontier firms over the index.
insights.quote: the gap between firms capturing value and growing and the rest is already stark and likely to widen further without targeted intervention
insights.locator: Put all this together and a single thread

insights.claim: A smaller group of ambitious, tech-forward businesses is separating from a much larger group that is neither growing nor shrinking but just holding on.
insights.speaker: Raoul Ruparel
insights.so_what: The UK economy's problem is dispersion, so index-level UK exposure captures the stagnant majority while missing the compounding frontier.
